claims.text: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a simple solid-solution state has relatively low hardness and strength.
The starting CoCrFeNiTi solid solution has minimal or no significant short-range order.
The absence of significant SRO causes the relatively low hardness and strength of the starting alloy.
SRO can act as a barrier to dislocation motion.
Freer dislocation motion explains the favorable plasticity and machinability of the starting CoCrFeNiTi alloy.
A targeted annealing treatment can promote SRO in CoCrFeNiTi without inducing secondary-phase precipitation.
The relevant structural mediator consists of nanoscopic SRO clusters that act as dislocation-pinning sites.
Slip through an SRO-containing alloy creates diffuse antiphase boundaries by destroying SRO on the slip plane.
The energy penalty and back stress associated with SRO and diffuse antiphase boundaries retard dislocation motion.
SRO-mediated resistance to dislocation motion enhances solid-solution strengthening.
Promoting SRO will increase both hardness and yield strength relative to the as-processed alloy.
Promoting SRO will reduce plastic strain or ductility.
The proposed mechanism applies from approximately 25 °C to 600 °C under moderate strain rates in uniaxial tensile or compression loading.
The proposed mechanism does not extend to multiphase or non-equimolar alloy systems.
TEM and XRD can provide evidence that the proposed annealing treatment increased SRO.
Using identically synthesized untreated and annealed samples provides a controlled comparison of their mechanical behavior.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis expressly includes nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi but also says it does not extend to non-equimolar alloy systems; a nearly equimolar composition is, strictly, non-equimolar.
